snip.t: Pancreas: β‑cells in the islets of Langerhans secrete insulin; α‑cells secrete glucagon. — Loss of insulin and relative glucagon excess drives lipolysis and gluconeogenesis.
Insulin deficiency → ↑ glucagon → ↑ hepatic gluconeogenesis & glycogenolysis → ↑ blood glucose
Insulin receptors on muscle, adipose and hepatic cells mediate glucose uptake, glycogen synthesis and inhibition of gluconeogenesis.
Other specific: Drug‑induced (e.g., protease inhibitors) → mitochondrial toxicity → impaired insulin signalling; endocrine tumours → excess counter‑regulatory hormones → hepatic gluconeogenesis ↑.

ai.subject: Biochemistry & genetics
ai.summary: Gluconeogenesis creates glucose from non‑carbohydrate precursors, crucial during fasting or stress. It shares most steps with glycolysis but uses distinct enzymes at key regulatory points.

sections.p: The liver (and to a lesser extent kidney) synthesises glucose when dietary supply is low, using lactate, glycerol, alanine and other substrates.
b: Provides blood glucose for brain and red cells during prolonged fasting.
Requires ATP and NAD⁺, making it energy‑intensive.

sections.p: Seven of the ten steps are identical to glycolysis; three are bypass reactions catalysed by fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase, phosphoenolpyruvate carboxykinase (PEPCK) and glucose‑6‑phosphatase.
b: Glycerol → DHAP (glycerol kinase, GPDH) enters glycolytic middle.

t.b: Is lactate being used as a substrate? High lactate with low glucose suggests impaired gluconeogenesis.
Detect accumulation of intermediates (e.g., pyruvate) that indicate enzyme block.

sections.p: Hormones and energy status control the three bypass enzymes. Glucagon, cortisol and catecholamines stimulate; insulin suppresses.
b: Fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase is inhibited by AMP and activated by citrate.
PEPCK transcription is up‑regulated by glucagon‑cAMP‑CREB pathway.
Alcohol raises NADH/NAD⁺, blocking conversion of lactate to pyruvate.

t.b: Is cortisol excess driving gluconeogenesis? Elevated cortisol explains hyperglycaemia in Cushing's.
High ratio indicates alcohol‑induced inhibition of gluconeogenesis.

sections.p: Defects in key enzymes or overwhelming substrate depletion cause hypoglycaemia, especially in newborns or critically ill patients.
b: Fructose‑1,6‑bisphosphatase deficiency → fasting hypoglycaemia, lactic acidosis.
Severe liver failure → loss of all gluconeogenic capacity.
Alcoholic binge → NADH excess blocks lactate utilisation.

sections.p: Understanding gluconeogenesis guides management of hypoglycaemia, diabetes, and critical illness.
b: In sepsis, high cortisol and catecholamines drive gluconeogenesis, raising glucose and insulin resistance.
In Cushing's or pheochromocytoma, excess hormones increase glucose production, worsening diabetes.
In malnutrition, preserving gluconeogenic substrates (protein) is vital.

t.b: Rising glucose despite fasting suggests hormonal excess; falling glucose signals inadequate gluconeogenesis.
Low albumin, elevated transaminases indicate hepatic inability to perform gluconeogenesis.

sections.p: Key points frequently tested in exams.
b: Name the three enzymes unique to gluconeogenesis.
Differentiate regulation by insulin vs glucagon.

whenToSeekHelp: Severe fasting hypoglycaemia (<40 mg/dL) with seizures or loss of consciousness
Acute liver failure with rising ammonia and encephalopathy
Unexplained lactic acidosis in an alcoholic patient

faq.q: Why does gluconeogenesis require more ATP than glycolysis?
faq.a: Two ATP are used to convert pyruvate to oxaloacetate and PEP, plus GTP for PEPCK, making it energetically costly.
Yes, especially during prolonged fasting; renal cortex uses glutamine and lactate.

faq.q: How does cortisol affect blood glucose?
faq.a: Cortisol up‑regulates PEPCK and other enzymes, increasing glucose output and causing insulin resistance.
